sentences: This bill is part of a package that creates the Trade Support Loans Programme, which provides concessional, income-contingent loans to apprentices.
The loans have a lifetime limit of $20,000 (indexed from 2017) and are repayable when the borrower's income reaches the HELP repayment threshold.
A 20% discount on the loan is applied when an Australian Apprentice successfully completes their apprenticeship.
changes: Establishes the Trade Support Loans Programme.
Sets a $20,000 lifetime loan limit, indexed from 2017.
Provides a 20% loan discount upon successful completion of an apprenticeship.
Makes loans repayable when income reaches the HELP repayment threshold.
Makes consequential amendments to existing legislation via the related bill.
summary.affected: Australian Apprentices who need financial support to cover personal costs during their apprenticeship.

divisions.question: The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2014-06-24.19.1) proposed by Liberal Minister [Christopher Pyne](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/sturt/christopher_pyne). The majority agreed to add Labor Senator [Kim Carr](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/kim_carr)'s [proviso](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-07-14.25.2) to the [motion](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/senate/2014-07-14/10) to agree with the bills' main idea. ### What was Senator Kim Carr's proviso? Trade Support Loans Bill 2014, Trade Support Loans (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2014 - Second Reading - Agree to the main idea (with two provisos)

The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-07-14.167.1) introduced by Greens Senator [Lee Rhiannon](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nsw/lee_rhiannon). ### What were the amendments? Senator Rhiannon [explained](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-07-14.167.1) that the amendments would have "increase[d] the repayment income threshold and provide[d] for lower repayment rates". ### Main idea of the bills The bills create the Trade Support Loans Programme that will give apprentices access to a $20,000 loan, like the loans already available for university students under [HECS](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education_fees_in_Australia#HECS). ### Background to the bills Prime Minister [Tony Abbott](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/tony_abbott) [promised to create](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-07-27/apprentice-loan-promise-check/5519824) this new loan programme during the [2013 election campaign](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_federal_election,_2013).

speeches.speaker: Ian Macfarlane
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of the Trade Support Loans Bill, providing apprentices up to $20,000 over four years from 1 July 2014 with a 20 per cent discount for completion, at an estimated $439 million impact on the fiscal balance, aimed at cutting dropout rates of 20 per cent in the first year and 30 per cent by the second.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill, recalling their own 1974 apprenticeship on a starting wage of $39 a week, and said their electorate of Swan has 5,184 apprentices, the fifth-highest of any electorate, even as Western Australian apprenticeship commencements fell 10.1 per cent in the 12 months to the end of 2013.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Defended the Trade Support Loans as a key election commitment, not a broken promise, saying the government would invest $1.9 billion in loans of up to $20,000 over the forward estimates at a cost of around $439 million.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Criticised the government for scrapping the $1 billion Tools For Your Trade program without telling apprentices before the election, and for cutting $5 billion from university funding, which they said would force fee rises of 40 to 60 per cent.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans as ending a two-tier system that favoured university students, blamed a past Victorian Labor government for abolishing technical secondary schools, and said their electorate of Murray has 3,055 apprentices in training who will be eligible for loans of up to $20,000.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill, and said constituents at regional shows across the electorate, including pensioners, self-funded retirees and young mothers, were angry and felt deceived by the budget, particularly the $7 GP tax.

speeches.speaker: Tony Smith
speeches.brief: Raised a point of order that the member had not yet addressed the substance of the Trade Support Loans Bill and should move on from the preamble about country shows to speak to the bill itself.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill, saying there were 8,534 people undertaking apprenticeships across the Central Coast and Hunter region, about 16 per cent of all apprentices in New South Wales, and quoted local employer Karen Drinan welcoming the loans to help cover tools, TAFE fees and transport.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Accused the government of halving the Tools For Your Trade program from $1 billion to $476 million over four years, read emails from apprentices objecting to the mid-apprenticeship change, and warned a newly qualified carpenter could take 34 years to repay the full loan.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Said the government's loans scheme effectively strips $561 million from apprentices, and cited Newcastle's NovaSkill mentoring program, which is being axed despite keeping apprentice attrition under 10 per cent against a 48 per cent national rate.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Criticised the industry minister's comments about apprentices misusing Tools For Your Trade funds, which were picked up by the Daily Mail under a headline claiming apprentices were spending '$1 billion in government grants for tools on whatever', and cited a National Centre for Vocational Education Research paper finding workplace treatment, not wages alone, drives non-completion.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill with reservations, praising Newcastle hairdressing salon owner Heather of Feathers for employing apprentices for more than 20 years, and criticised the government for axing the Australian Apprenticeships Mentoring Program and Access Program alongside Tools For Your Trade.

speeches.speaker: Rob Mitchell
speeches.brief: Opposed the Trade Support Loans Bill as a broken promise, quoting a Sydney Morning Herald report from August 2013 confirming the coalition promised the loans would be 'in addition to' Tools For Your Trade, and said almost $2 billion had been cut from apprentice and worker support programs in this budget.

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill, arguing the net present value of a $20,000 loan with a $4,000 completion discount far exceeds the old $5,500 Tools For Your Trade payment, and that low apprentice wages compared with peers working at fast food outlets were a key reason for high dropout rates.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: Opposed the Trade Support Loans Bill, detailing how the Victorian Liberal government's $170 million cut to TAFE funding had led to the retrenchment of more than 13 student support workers at Victoria University, whose TAFE arm lost over 25 per cent of its funding, hitting disadvantaged students in Melbourne's west hardest.

speeches.speaker: Brett Whiteley
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill for his Braddon electorate, noting loans are repayable once apprentices earn about $53,000 and cover more than 60 eligible trades, and cited a Devonport Chamber of Commerce report on the need to better match apprentice training to local industry needs like dairying and berry growing.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Opposed the Trade Support Loans Bill, recounting mature-age electrical apprentice Greg's account of working for $7.50 an hour while raising a family, and defended the Outer Northern Trade Training Centre in his Lalor electorate against claims such centres failed to match local industry needs.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Moved a debate management motion capping debate on the Trade Support Loans Bill 2014 at 45 minutes for the second reading and 20 minutes for consideration in detail, calling the bill a signature budget measure letting apprentices borrow from taxpayers to complete their training.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: Defended the Trade Support Loans Bill, saying Labor's Tools For Your Trade program had a 50 per cent apprentice drop-out rate, and touted loans of up to $20,000 plus a $4,000 bonus for apprentices who complete their training.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Criticised the Trade Support Loans Bill for scrapping the $1 billion Tools For Your Trade program without warning before the election and replacing it with loans of up to $20,000, and read a constituent's letter describing an apprentice carpenter earning just $14.50 an hour who would struggle with such a debt.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Defended the Trade Support Loans as addressing a 50 per cent apprentice drop-out rate, and said loans of up to $20,000 need not be repaid until an apprentice's income exceeds $50,000 a year.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Summed up the Trade Support Loans Bill debate, rejecting Labor's amendments, and said loans of up to $20,000 need not be repaid until income exceeds $50,000 a year, with about half of the roughly 149,000 apprentices currently in high-priority training expected to complete their courses.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: Supported the Trade Support Loans Bill, citing an estimated $1.9 billion in loans over four years to help apprentices afford tools, and described how excessive red and green tape had led one Queensland contractor, who trained 39 electricians since 1986, to stop taking on new apprentices.
